Source: https://github.com/hed-standard/hed-schemas. Hermes et al., Scientific Data (2025), https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-025-05791-2. Modified: reduced to the SCORE terms and the standard's artifact terms, their placeholders and units, and rewritten as JSON.

terms.name: Modulator
terms.description: External stimuli / interventions or changes in the alertness level (sleep) that modify: the background activity, or how often a graphoelement is occurring, or change other features of the graphoelement (like intra-burst frequency). For each observed feature, there is an option of specifying how they are influenced by the modulators and procedures that were done during the recording.

terms.name: Sleep-modulator
terms.description: When sleep/drowsiness features are scored during drowsiness, Drowsy should be listed as a modulator

terms.name: Hyperventilation
terms.description: When selecting hyperventilation from the list, the user is prompted to score the quality of the hyperventilation (excellent effort, good effort, poor effort, refused the procedure, unable to do the procedure).

terms.name: Other-modulator-or-procedure
terms.description: Free text describing other modulators or procedures.

terms.name: Background-activity
terms.description: An EEG activity representing the setting in which a given normal or abnormal pattern appears and from which such pattern is distinguished.

terms.name: Posterior-dominant-rhythm
terms.description: Rhythmic activity occurring during wakefulness over the posterior regions of the head, generally with maximum amplitudes over the occipital areas. Amplitude varies. Best seen with eyes closed and during physical relaxation and relative mental inactivity. Blocked or attenuated by attention, especially visual, and mental effort. In adults this is the alpha rhythm, and the frequency is 8 to 13 Hz. However the frequency can be higher or lower than this range (often a supra or sub harmonic of alpha frequency) and is called alpha variant rhythm (fast and slow alpha variant rhythm). In children, the normal range of the frequency of the posterior dominant rhythm is age-dependant.

terms.name: Mu-rhythm
terms.description: EEG rhythm at 7-11 Hz composed of arch-shaped waves occurring over the central or centro-parietal regions of the scalp during wakefulness. Amplitudes varies but is mostly below 50 microV. Blocked or attenuated most clearly by contralateral movement, thought of movement, readiness to move or tactile stimulation.

terms.name: Other-organized-rhythm
terms.description: EEG activity consisting of waves of approximately constant period that are considered part of the background (ongoing) activity, but do not fulfill the criteria of the posterior dominant rhythm.

terms.name: Background-activity-special-feature
terms.description: Special features provide scoring options for the background activity of critically ill patients.

terms.name: Background-burst-suppression
terms.description: EEG pattern consisting of bursts (activity appearing and disappearing abruptly) interrupted by periods of low amplitude (below 20 microV). This pattern occurs simultaneously over all head regions.

terms.name: Background-activity-suppression
terms.description: Periods showing activity under 10 microV (referential montage) and interrupting the background (ongoing) activity.

terms.name: Electrocerebral-inactivity
terms.description: Absence of any ongoing cortical electric activities; in all leads EEG is isoelectric or only contains artifacts. Sensitivity has to be increased up to 2 microV/mm; recording time: at least 30 minutes.

terms.name: Critically-ill-patient-patterns
terms.description: Rhythmic or periodic patterns in critically ill patients (RPPs) are scored according to the 2012 version of the American Clinical Neurophysiology Society Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology.

terms.name: Critically-ill-patient-periodic-discharges
terms.description: Periodic discharges (PDs): Periodic - repetition of a waveform with relatively uniform morphology and duration with a quantifiable inter-discharge interval between consecutive waveforms and recurrence of the waveform at nearly regular intervals.

terms.name: Rhythmic-delta-activity
terms.description: Rhythmic Delta Activity (RDA): Rhythmic - repetition of a waveform with relatively uniform morphology and duration, and without an interval between consecutive waveforms. RDA - rhythmic activity less than or equal to 4 Hz. The duration of one cycle (i.e., the period) of the rhythmic pattern should vary by less than 50 percent from the duration of the subsequent cycle for the majority (greater than 50 percent) of cycle pairs to qualify as rhythmic.

terms.name: Spike-or-sharp-and-wave
terms.description: Spike-and-wave or Sharp-and-wave (SW) - polyspike, spike or sharp wave consistently followed by a slow wave in a regularly repeating and alternating pattern (spike-wave-spike-wave-spike-wave), with a consistent relationship between the spike (or polyspike or sharp wave) component and the slow wave; and with no interval between one spike-wave complex and the next (if there is an interval, this would qualify as PDs, where each discharge is a spike-and- wave).

terms.name: Episode
terms.description: Clinical episode or electrographic seizure.

terms.name: Epileptic-seizure
terms.description: The ILAE seizure classification divides seizures into focal, generalized onset, or unknown onset.

terms.name: Focal-onset-epileptic-seizure
terms.description: A focal seizure originates within networks limited to one hemisphere. They may be discretely localized or more widely distributed. Focal seizures may originate in subcortical structures. Focal seizures are optionally subdivided into focal aware and focal impaired awareness seizures. Specific motor and nonmotor classifiers may be added.

terms.name: Aware-focal-onset-epileptic-seizure
terms.description: Focal onset and maintained awareness (knowledge of self or environment).

terms.name: Impaired-awareness-focal-onset-epileptic-seizure
terms.description: Focal onset and impaired or lost awareness (knowledge of self or environment) is a feature of focal impaired awareness seizures, previously called complex partial seizures.

terms.name: Awareness-unknown-focal-onset-epileptic-seizure
terms.description: Focal onset and awareness (knowledge of self or environment) unknown or not specified.

terms.name: Focal-to-bilateral-tonic-clonic-focal-onset-epileptic-seizure
terms.description: A seizure type with focal onset, with awareness or impaired awareness, either motor or non-motor, progressing to bilateral tonic clonic activity. The prior term was seizure with partial onset with secondary generalization.

terms.name: Generalized-onset-epileptic-seizure
terms.description: Generalized seizures originate at some point within, and rapidly engaging, bilaterally distributed networks. Generalized onset seizures can be motor: tonic clonic, clonic, tonic, myoclonic, myoclonic tonic clonic, myoclonic atonic, atonic, and epileptic spasms. Generalized onset seizures can also be nonmotor (absence): typical absence, atypical absence, myoclonic absence, or absence with eyelid myoclonia.

terms.name: Unknown-onset-epileptic-seizure
terms.description: A seizure of unknown onset may still evidence certain defining motor (e.g., tonic clonic) or nonmotor (e.g., behavior arrest) characteristics. With further information or future observed seizures, a reclassification of unknown-onset seizures into focal or generalized-onset categories may become possible. Therefore, unknown onset is not a characteristic of the seizure, but a convenient placeholder for our ignorance.

terms.name: Unclassified-epileptic-seizure
terms.description: Referring to a seizure type that cannot be described by the ILAE 2017 classification either because of inadequate information or unusual clinical features.

terms.name: Electroencephalographic-seizure
terms.description: Refers usually to non convulsive status. Ictal EEG: rhythmic discharge or spike and wave pattern with definite evolution in frequency, location, or morphology lasting at least 10 s; evolution in amplitude alone did not qualify.

terms.name: Seizure-PNES
terms.description: Psychogenic non-epileptic seizure. Paroxysmal events that mimic (or are confused with) epileptic seizures, but which do not result from epileptic activity; they lack the EEG ictal features during the ictus.

terms.name: Sleep-related-arousal
terms.description: Normal arousal.

terms.name: Benign-sleep-myoclonus
terms.description: A distinctive disorder of sleep characterized by a) neonatal onset, b) rhythmic myoclonic jerks only during sleep and c) abrupt and consistent cessation with arousal, d) absence of concomitant electrographic changes suggestive of seizures, and e) good outcome.

terms.name: Confusional-arousal
terms.description: Episode of non epileptic nature included in NREM parasomnias, characterized by sudden arousal and complex behavior but without full alertness, usually lasting a few minutes and occurring almost in all children at least occasionally. Amnesia of the episode is the rule.

terms.name: Cataplexy
terms.description: A sudden decrement in muscle tone and loss of deep tendon reflexes, leading to muscle weakness, paralysis, or postural collapse. Cataplexy usually is precipitated by an outburst of emotional expression-notably laughter, anger, or startle. It is one of the tetrad of symptoms of narcolepsy. During cataplexy, respiration and voluntary eye movements are not compromised. Consciousness is preserved.

terms.name: Sleep-periodic-limb-movement
terms.description: PLMS (Periodic limb movement in sleep). Episodes are characterized by brief (0.5- to 5.0-second) lower-extremity movements during sleep, which typically occur at 20- to 40-second intervals, most commonly during the first 3 hours of sleep. The affected individual is usually not aware of the movements or of the transient partial arousals.

terms.name: REM-sleep-behavioral-disorder
terms.description: REM sleep behavioral disorder. Episodes characterized by: a) presence of REM sleep without atonia (RSWA) on polysomnography (PSG); b) presence of at least 1 of the following conditions - (1) Sleep-related behaviors, by history, that have been injurious, potentially injurious, or disruptive (example: dream enactment behavior); (2) abnormal REM sleep behavior documented during PSG monitoring; (3) absence of epileptiform activity on electroencephalogram (EEG) during REM sleep (unless RBD can be clearly distinguished from any concurrent REM sleep-related seizure disorder); (4) sleep disorder not better explained by another sleep disorder, a medical or neurologic disorder, a mental disorder, medication use, or a substance use disorder.

terms.name: Sleep-walking
terms.description: Episodes characterized by ambulation during sleep; the patient is difficult to arouse during an episode, and is usually amnesic following the episode. Episodes usually occur in the first third of the night during slow wave sleep. Polysomnographic recordings demonstrate 2 abnormalities during the first sleep cycle: frequent, brief, non-behavioral EEG-defined arousals prior to the somnambulistic episode and abnormally low gamma (0.75-2.0 Hz) EEG power on spectral analysis, correlating with high-voltage (hyper-synchronic gamma) waves lasting 10 to 15 s occurring just prior to the movement. This is followed by stage I NREM sleep, and there is no evidence of complete awakening.

terms.name: Hyperekplexia
terms.description: Disorder characterized by exaggerated startle response and hypertonicity that may occur during the first year of life and in severe cases during the neonatal period. Children usually present with marked irritability and recurrent startles in response to handling and sounds. Severely affected infants can have severe jerks and stiffening, sometimes with breath-holding spells.

terms.name: Jactatio-capitis-nocturna
terms.description: Relatively common in normal children at the time of going to bed, especially during the first year of life, the rhythmic head movements persist during sleep. Usually, these phenomena disappear before 3 years of age.

terms.name: Pavor-nocturnus
terms.description: A nocturnal episode characterized by age of onset of less than five years (mean age 18 months, with peak prevalence at five to seven years), appearance of signs of panic two hours after falling asleep with crying, screams, a fearful expression, inability to recognize other people including parents (for a duration of 5-15 minutes), amnesia upon awakening. Pavor nocturnus occurs in patients almost every night for months or years (but the frequency is highly variable and may be as low as once a month) and is likely to disappear spontaneously at the age of six to eight years.

terms.name: Pediatric-stereotypical-behavior-episode
terms.description: Repetitive motor behavior in children, typically rhythmic and persistent; usually not paroxysmal and rarely suggest epilepsy. They include headbanging, head-rolling, jactatio capitis nocturna, body rocking, buccal or lingual movements, hand flapping and related mannerisms, repetitive hand-waving (to self-induce photosensitive seizures).

terms.name: Paroxysmal-motor-event
terms.description: Paroxysmal phenomena during neonatal or childhood periods characterized by recurrent motor or behavioral signs or symptoms that must be distinguished from epileptic disorders.

terms.name: Syncope
terms.description: Episode with loss of consciousness and muscle tone that is abrupt in onset, of short duration and followed by rapid recovery; it occurs in response to transient impairment of cerebral perfusion. Typical prodromal symptoms often herald onset of syncope and postictal symptoms are minimal. Syncopal convulsions resulting from cerebral anoxia are common but are not a form of epilepsy, nor are there any accompanying EEG ictal discharges.

terms.name: Feature-property
terms.description: Descriptive element similar to main HED /Property. Something that pertains to a thing. A characteristic of some entity. A quality or feature regarded as a characteristic or inherent part of someone or something. HED attributes are adjectives or adverbs.

terms.name: Signal-morphology-property
terms.description: Signal morphology attributes relevant to features of background, interictal or ictal activity.

terms.name: Rhythmic-property
terms.description: Rhythmic activity can be observed during background, interictal or ictal activity and HED-SCORE therefore describes this as an property/attribute.

terms.name: Delta-activity
terms.description: Rhythmic activity in the delta frequency range (under 4 Hz).

terms.name: Theta-activity
terms.description: Rhythmic activity in the theta frequency range (4-8 Hz).

terms.name: Alpha-activity
terms.description: Rhythmic activity in the alpha frequency range (8-13 Hz), but not a part of the posterior dominant rhythm.

terms.name: Beta-activity
terms.description: Rhythmic activity in the beta frequency range (14-40 Hz).

terms.name: Gamma-activity
terms.description: Rhythmic activity in the gamma frequency range.

terms.name: Polymorphic-delta-activity
terms.description: EEG activity consisting of waves in the delta range (over 250 ms duration for each wave) but of different morphology.

terms.name: Frontal-intermittent-rhythmic-delta-activity
terms.description: Frontal intermittent rhythmic delta activity (FIRDA). Fairly regular or approximately sinusoidal waves, mostly occurring in bursts at 1.5-2.5 Hz over the frontal areas of one or both sides of the head. Comment: most commonly associated with unspecified encephalopathy, in adults.

terms.name: Occipital-intermittent-rhythmic-delta-activity
terms.description: Occipital intermittent rhythmic delta activity (OIRDA). Fairly regular or approximately sinusoidal waves, mostly occurring in bursts at 2-3 Hz over the occipital or posterior head regions of one or both sides of the head. Frequently blocked or attenuated by opening the eyes. Comment: most commonly associated with unspecified encephalopathy, in children.

terms.name: Temporal-intermittent-rhythmic-delta-activity
terms.description: Temporal intermittent rhythmic delta activity (TIRDA). Fairly regular or approximately sinusoidal waves, mostly occurring in bursts at over the temporal areas of one side of the head. Comment: most commonly associated with temporal lobe epilepsy.

terms.name: Spike
terms.description: A transient, clearly distinguished from background activity, with pointed peak at a conventional paper speed or time scale and duration from 20 to under 70 ms, i.e. 1/50-1/15 s approximately. Main component is generally negative relative to other areas. Amplitude varies.

terms.name: Spike-and-slow-wave
terms.description: A pattern consisting of a spike followed by a slow wave.

terms.name: Runs-of-rapid-spikes
terms.description: Bursts of spike discharges at a rate from 10 to 25/sec (in most cases somewhat irregular). The bursts last more than 2 seconds (usually 2 to 10 seconds) and the runs are typically seen in sleep. Synonyms: rhythmic spikes, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, fast paroxysmal rhythms, grand mal discharge, fast beta activity.

terms.name: Polyspikes
terms.description: Two or more consecutive spikes.

terms.name: Polyspike-and-slow-wave
terms.description: Two or more consecutive spikes associated with one or more slow waves.

terms.name: Sharp-wave
terms.description: A transient clearly distinguished from background activity, with pointed peak at a conventional paper speed or time scale, and duration of 70-200 ms, i.e. over 1/4-1/5 s approximately. Main component is generally negative relative to other areas. Amplitude varies.

terms.name: Sharp-and-slow-wave
terms.description: A sequence of a sharp wave and a slow wave.

terms.name: Slow-sharp-wave
terms.description: A transient that bears all the characteristics of a sharp-wave, but exceeds 200 ms. Synonym: blunted sharp wave.

terms.name: High-frequency-oscillation
terms.description: High Frequency Oscillation (HFO). Oscillations with a frequency higher than 80 Hz.

terms.name: Hypsarrhythmia-classic
terms.description: Pattern consisting of diffuse chaotic high voltage (more than 300 ??V) irregular slow waves interspersed with multiregional spikes and sharp waves over both hemispheres.

terms.name: Hypsarrhythmia-modified
terms.description: Pattern consisting of diffuse chaotic high voltage (more than 300 ??V) irregular slow waves interspersed with multiregional spikes and sharp waves over both hemispheres.

terms.name: Fast-spike-activity
terms.description: A burst consisting of a sequence of spikes. Duration greater than 1 s. Frequency at least in the alpha range.

terms.name: Low-voltage-fast-activity
terms.description: Refers to the fast, and often recruiting activity which can be recorded at the onset of an ictal discharge, particularly in invasive EEG recording of a seizure.

terms.name: Polysharp-waves
terms.description: A sequence of two or more sharp-waves.

terms.name: Slow-wave-large-amplitude
terms.description: Slow wave of large amplitude.

terms.name: Irregular-delta-or-theta-activity
terms.description: EEG activity consisting of repetitive waves of inconsistent wave-duration but in delta and/or theta range (greater than 125 ms).

terms.name: Electrodecremental-change
terms.description: Sudden desynchronization of electrical activity.

terms.name: DC-shift
terms.description: Shift of negative polarity of the direct current recordings, during seizures.

terms.name: Disappearance-of-ongoing-activity
terms.description: Disappearance of the EEG activity that preceded the ictal event but still remnants of background activity (thus not enough to name it electrodecremental change).

terms.name: RPP-morphology
terms.description: Modifier terms for Rhythmic or Periodic Patterns in critically ill patients (RPPs).

terms.name: RPP-with-superimposed-activity
terms.description: Superimposed activity (for PDs and RDA).

terms.name: Superimposed-fast-activity
terms.description: Superimposed fast activity.

terms.name: Superimposed-rhythmic-activity
terms.description: Superimposed rhythmic activity (for PDs only).

terms.name: Superimposed-sharp-waves-or-spikes
terms.description: Superimposed sharp waves or spikes (for RDA only).

terms.name: RPP-sharpness
terms.description: Sharpness (for PDs and SW).

terms.name: RPP-spiky
terms.description: Spiky (<70 ms, measured at the baseline). )

terms.name: RPP-sharp
terms.description: Sharp (70-200 ms).

terms.name: RPP-sharply-contoured
terms.description: Sharply contoured.

terms.name: RPP-blunt
terms.description: Blunt.

terms.name: Number-of-RPP-phases
terms.description: Number of phases (for PDs and SW): 1, 2 or 3.

terms.name: Triphasic-morphology
terms.description: Waves with three distinct phases (for PDs and SW).

terms.name: RPP-absolute-amplitude
terms.description: Absolute amplitude (for PDs, RDA, SW). Can use suggested tags for amplitude range. Very low, (Feature-amplitude, (Less-than, (Feature-amplitude/20 uv))): less than 20 microV, Low: 20 to 49 microV, Medium: 50 to 199 microV, High: Greater than 200 microV.

terms.name: RPP-relative-amplitude
terms.description: Relative amplitude (for PDs), should indicate if it's less than or equal to 2 or greater than 2.

terms.name: RPP-polarity
terms.description: Polarity (for PDs and SW).

terms.name: RPP-tangential-polarity
terms.description: Tangential/horizontal dipole.

terms.name: Sensor-list
terms.description: Lists all corresponding sensors (electrodes/channels in montage). The sensor-group is selected from a list defined in the site-settings for each EEG-lab.

terms.name: Source-analysis-property
terms.description: In case source imaging is done, the results are scored at sublobar level: frontal (perisylvian-superior surface; lateral; mesial; polar; orbitofrontal), temporal (polar; basal, lateral-anterior; lateral-posterior; perisylvian-inferior surface), central (lateral convexity; mesial; central sulcus-anterior surface, central sulcus-posterior surface; opercular), parietal (lateral-convexity; mesial; opercular), occipital (lateral; mesial, basal) and insula.

terms.name: Location-property
terms.description: Location can be scored for features. Semiologic feature can also be characterized by the somatotopic modifier (i.e. the part of the body where it occurs). In this respect, laterality (left, right, symmetric, asymmetric, left greater than right, right greater than left), body part (eyelid, face, arm, leg, trunk, visceral, left/right) and centricity (axial (trunk), proximal limb, distal limb).

terms.name: Feature-propagation
terms.description: When propagation within the graphoelement is observed, first the location of the onset region is scored. Then, the location of the propagation can be noted.

terms.name: Multifocal-feature
terms.description: When the same interictal graphoelement is observed bilaterally and at least in three independent locations, can score them using one entry, and choosing multifocal as a descriptor of the locations of the given interictal graphoelements, optionally emphasizing the involved, and the most active sites.

terms.name: Modulators-property
terms.description: For each described graphoelement, the influence of the modulators can be scored. Only modulators present in the recording are scored.

terms.name: Modulators-reactivity
terms.description: Susceptibility of individual rhythms or the EEG as a whole to change following sensory stimulation or other physiologic actions. The type of stimulus can be a modulator or can be specified in free-text.

terms.name: Facilitating-factor
terms.description: The facilitating factors (if known) can be selected: alcohol (Suggested tag: Intoxicated), awakening, catamenial, fever, sleep, sleep-deprivation, other (free text). Facilitating factors are defined as transient and sporadic endogenous or exogenous elements capable of augmenting seizure incidence (increasing the likelihood of seizure occurrence).

terms.name: Provocative-factor
terms.description: Provocative factors are defined as transient and sporadic endogenous or exogenous elements capable of evoking/triggering seizures immediately following the exposure to it.

terms.name: Intermittent-photic-stimulation-effect
terms.description: The effect of Intermittent Photic Stimulation (IPS) is scored according to the terminology proposed by Kasteleijn-Nolst Trenite ea (2001).

terms.name: Posterior-stimulus-dependent-response
terms.description: Anomalous steady-state VEPs, of unusually sharp waveform or high amplitude. Some types have clinical correlates, for instance, occipital spikes after suppression of generalized PPR by medication and high-amplitude VEPs in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.

terms.name: Posterior-stimulus-independent-response-limited
terms.description: Limited to the stimulus train: Activity confined to or maximal at the back of the head and not at the flash frequency or at a harmonic thereof. The term includes delta and theta activity and frank epileptiform patterns.

terms.name: Posterior-stimulus-independent-response-self-sustained
terms.description: Self-sustaining: Self-sustaining posterior stimulus-independent responses that outlast the stimulus train. These often last many seconds and may evolve to an overt seizure.

terms.name: Generalized-photoparoxysmal-response-limited
terms.description: Limited to the stimulus train: Comprises multiple spikes or spike-and-wave activity, which are apparently generalized, but may be of greater amplitude at the front or back of the head. It is termed a photoconvulsive response (PCR) by Bickford et al., and corresponds to type 4 response of Waltz et al.

terms.name: Generalized-photoparoxysmal-response-self-sustained
terms.description: Self-sustaining: Generalized PPR continuing after stimulation. This may not be demonstrated unless the stimulus train is terminated as soon as a generalized PPR is identified. It was termed prolonged photoconvulsive response by Reilly and Peters, and has a strong association with epilepsy and visually induced seizures in patients referred for clinical EEG examination. Its prevalence in asymptomatic general populations is unknown, but was found in five of 13,658 apparently healthy aircrew by Gregory et al.

terms.name: Activation-of-pre-existing-epileptogenic-area
terms.description: Rarely, photic stimulation may activate an epileptogenic cortex, which is also spontaneously active; IPS could then also elicit a seizure by stimulating this, usually posterior located, area. It is questionable whether this should be considered a photoparoxysmal response (PPR), and it does not figure in established classifications.

terms.name: Time-related-property
terms.description: Estimates of how often a graphoelement is seen in the recording.

terms.name: Appearance-mode
terms.description: Describes how the non-ictal EEG pattern/graphoelement is distributed through the recording. Occurrence of the non-ictal EEG pattern / graphoelement can be Random, Repetitive or Varying. Random: occurring without any rhythmicity / periodicity, Repetitive: occurring at an approximately regular rate / interval (generally of 1 to several seconds). Variable: occurring sometimes rhythmic or periodic, other times random, throughout the recording.)

terms.name: Discharge-pattern
terms.description: Describes the organization of the EEG signal within the discharge (distinguish between single and repetitive discharges).

terms.name: Single-discharge
terms.description: Applies to the intra-burst pattern: a graphoelement that is not repetitive; before and after the graphoelement one can distinguish the background activity.

terms.name: Rhythmic-trains-or-bursts
terms.description: Applies to the intra-burst pattern: a non-ictal graphoelement that repeats itself without returning to the background activity between them. The graphoelements within this repetition occur at approximately constant period.

terms.name: Arrhythmic-trains-or-bursts
terms.description: Applies to the intra-burst pattern: a non-ictal graphoelement that repeats itself without returning to the background activity between them. The graphoelements within this repetition occur at inconstant period.

terms.name: RPP-time-related-feature
terms.description: Time related feature for Rhythmic or Periodic Patterns in critically ill patients (RPPs).

terms.name: RPP-duration
terms.description: Duration (for PDs, RDA and SW). The suggestedTag Property-not-possible-to-determine may be used if it is not possible to determine.

terms.name: Very-brief-RPP-duration
terms.description: Less than 10 sec.

terms.name: Brief-RPP-duration
terms.description: 10 to 59 sec.

terms.name: Intermediate-RPP-duration
terms.description: 1 to 4.9 min.

terms.name: Long-RPP-duration
terms.description: 5 to 59 min.

terms.name: Very-long-RPP-duration
terms.description: Greater than 1 hour.

terms.name: RPP-onset
terms.description: Onset (for PDs, RDA and SW). The suggestedTag Property-not-possible-to-determine may be used if it is not possible to determine.

terms.name: Sudden-RPP-onset
terms.description: Sudden (progressing from absent to well developed within 3 s.

terms.name: Gradual-RPP-onset
terms.description: Gradual onset.

terms.name: RPP-dynamics
terms.description: Dynamics (for PDs, RDA and SW). The suggestedTag Property-not-possible-to-determine may be used if it is not possible to determine.

terms.name: Feature-incidence
terms.description: For single discharges, estimates of how often features are seen in the recording are scored as incidence (how often it occurs/time-epoch).

terms.name: Rare-feature-incidence
terms.description: Less than 1/h.

terms.name: Uncommon-feature-incidence
terms.description: 1/5 min to 1/h.

terms.name: Occasional-feature-incidence
terms.description: 1/min to 1/5min.

terms.name: Frequent-feature-incidence
terms.description: 1/10 s to 1/min.

terms.name: Abundant-feature-incidence
terms.description: Greater than 1/10 s. (Source: Beniczky ea 2017, Table 6.)

terms.name: Feature-prevalence
terms.description: For trains or bursts, estimates of how often features are seen in the recording are scored as prevalence (the percentage of the recording covered by the train/burst).

terms.name: Rare-prevalence
terms.description: Less than 1 percent.

terms.name: Occasional-prevalence
terms.description: 1 to 9 percent.

terms.name: Frequent-prevalence
terms.description: 10 to 49 percent.

terms.name: Abundant-prevalence
terms.description: 50 to 89 percent.

terms.name: Continuous-prevalence
terms.description: Greater than 90 percent.

terms.name: Posterior-dominant-rhythm-property
terms.description: Posterior dominant rhythm is the most often scored EEG feature in clinical practice. Therefore, there are specific terms that can be chosen for characterizing the PDR. Note that frequency and amplitude can be further described to be symmetrical or asymmetrical.

terms.name: Posterior-dominant-rhythm-amplitude-range
terms.description: Low: less than 20 microV, Medium: 20 to 70 microVSource, High: more than 70 microV.

terms.name: Posterior-dominant-rhythm-eye-opening-reactivity
terms.description: Change (disappearance or measurable decrease in amplitude) of a posterior dominant rhythm following eye-opening. Eye closure has the opposite effect.

terms.name: Posterior-dominant-rhythm-organization
terms.description: Posterior dominant rhythm organization. When normal could be labeled with suggested tag.

terms.name: Posterior-dominant-rhythm-organization-poorly-organized
terms.description: Poorly organized.

terms.name: Posterior-dominant-rhythm-organization-disorganized
terms.description: Disorganized.

terms.name: Posterior-dominant-rhythm-organization-markedly-disorganized
terms.description: Markedly disorganized.

terms.name: Posterior-dominant-rhythm-caveat
terms.description: Caveats for PDR annotation, use suggestedTags to indicate whether there were: no caveats, only open eyes during the recording, sleep-deprived, drowsy or only following hyperventilation.

terms.name: Absence-of-posterior-dominant-rhythm
terms.description: Reason for absence of PDR.

terms.name: Absence-of-posterior-dominant-rhythm-other-causes
terms.description: annotation=dc:source Beniczky ea 2017 Table 4.

terms.name: Episode-property
terms.description: Episode property pertains to the set of characteristics that collectively depict different aspects of an episode, encompassing its manifestations and phases.

terms.name: Seizure-classification
terms.description: Seizure classification refers to the grouping of seizures based on their clinical features, EEG patterns, and other characteristics. Epileptic seizures are named using the current ILAE seizure classification.

terms.name: Myoclonic-seizure
terms.description: Sudden, brief (lower than 100 msec) involuntary single or multiple contraction(s) of muscles(s) or muscle groups of variable topography (axial, proximal limb, distal). Myoclonus is less regularly repetitive and less sustained than is clonus. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Negative-myoclonic-seizure
terms.description: annotation=dc:source Beniczky ea 2017 Supplement 1, annotation=dc:source Duration tag from Beniczky ea Table 13

terms.name: Motor-seizure
terms.description: Involves musculature in any form. The motor event could consist of an increase (positive) or decrease (negative) in muscle contraction to produce a movement. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Clonic-seizure
terms.description: Jerking, either symmetric or asymmetric, that is regularly repetitive and involves the same muscle groups. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Tonic-seizure
terms.description: A sustained increase in muscle contraction lasting a few seconds to minutes. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Atonic-seizure
terms.description: Sudden loss or diminution of muscle tone without apparent preceding myoclonic or tonic event lasting about 1 to 2 s, involving head, trunk, jaw, or limb musculature. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Myoclonic-atonic-seizure
terms.description: A generalized seizure type with a myoclonic jerk leading to an atonic motor component. This type was previously called myoclonic astatic. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Myoclonic-tonic-clonic-seizure
terms.description: One or a few jerks of limbs bilaterally, followed by a tonic clonic seizure. The initial jerks can be considered to be either a brief period of clonus or myoclonus. Seizures with this characteristic are common in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Tonic-clonic-seizure
terms.description: A sequence consisting of a tonic followed by a clonic phase. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Automatism-seizure
terms.description: A more or less coordinated motor activity usually occurring when cognition is impaired and for which the subject is usually (but not always) amnesic afterward. This often resembles a voluntary movement and may consist of an inappropriate continuation of preictal motor activity. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Epileptic-spasm
terms.description: A sudden flexion, extension, or mixed extension flexion of predominantly proximal and truncal muscles that is usually more sustained than a myoclonic movement but not as sustained as a tonic seizure. Limited forms may occur: Grimacing, head nodding, or subtle eye movements. Epileptic spasms frequently occur in clusters. Infantile spasms are the best known form, but spasms can occur at all ages. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Nonmotor-seizure
terms.description: Focal or generalized seizure types in which motor activity is not prominent. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Behavior-arrest-seizure
terms.description: Arrest (pause) of activities, freezing, immobilization, as in behavior arrest seizure. A focal behavior arrest seizure shows arrest of behavior as the prominent feature of the entire seizure. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Sensory-seizure
terms.description: A perceptual experience not caused by appropriate stimuli in the external world. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Emotional-seizure
terms.description: Seizures presenting with an emotion or the appearance of having an emotion as an early prominent feature, such as fear, spontaneous joy or euphoria, laughing (gelastic), or crying (dacrystic). Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Cognitive-seizure
terms.description: Pertaining to thinking and higher cortical functions, such as language, spatial perception, memory, and praxis. The previous term for similar usage as a seizure type was psychic. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Autonomic-seizure
terms.description: A distinct alteration of autonomic nervous system function involving cardiovascular, pupillary, gastrointestinal, sudomotor, vasomotor, and thermoregulatory functions. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Absence-seizure
terms.description: Absence seizures present with a sudden cessation of activity and awareness. Absence seizures tend to occur in younger age groups, have more sudden start and termination, and they usually display less complex automatisms than do focal seizures with impaired awareness, but the distinctions are not absolute. EEG information may be required for accurate classification. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Typical-absence-seizure
terms.description: A sudden onset, interruption of ongoing activities, a blank stare, possibly a brief upward deviation of the eyes. Usually the patient will be unresponsive when spoken to. Duration is a few seconds to half a minute with very rapid recovery. Although not always available, an EEG would show generalized epileptiform discharges during the event. An absence seizure is by definition a seizure of generalized onset. The word is not synonymous with a blank stare, which also can be encountered with focal onset seizures. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Atypical-absence-seizure
terms.description: An absence seizure with changes in tone that are more pronounced than in typical absence or the onset and/or cessation is not abrupt, often associated with slow, irregular, generalized spike-wave activity. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Myoclonic-absence-seizure
terms.description: A myoclonic absence seizure refers to an absence seizure with rhythmic three-per-second myoclonic movements, causing ratcheting abduction of the upper limbs leading to progressive arm elevation, and associated with three-per-second generalized spike-wave discharges. Duration is typically 10 to 60 s. Impairment of consciousness may not be obvious. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Eyelid-myoclonia-seizure
terms.description: Jerking of the eyelids at frequencies of at least 3 per second, commonly with upward eye deviation, usually lasting <10 s, often precipitated by eye closure. There may or may not be associated brief loss of awareness. Definition from ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types Expanded Version.

terms.name: Seizure-semiology
terms.description: Seizure semiology refers to the clinical signs and sympoms that are observed during a seizure. Semiology is described according to the ILAE Glossary of Descriptive Terminology for Ictal Semiology (Blume ea 2001). Besides the name, the semiologic feature can also be characterized by the somatotopic modifier, laterality, body part and centricity. Uses Location-property tags.

terms.name: Semiology-motor-behavioral-arrest
terms.description: Interruption of ongoing motor activity or of ongoing behaviors with fixed gaze, without movement of the head or trunk (oro-alimentary and hand automatisms may continue).

terms.name: Semiology-dyscognitive
terms.description: The term describes events in which (1) disturbance of cognition is the predominant or most apparent feature, and (2a) two or more of the following components are involved, or (2b) involvement of such components remains undetermined. Otherwise, use the more specific term (e.g., mnemonic experiential seizure or hallucinatory experiential seizure). Components of cognition: ++ perception: symbolic conception of sensory information ++ attention: appropriate selection of a principal perception or task ++ emotion: appropriate affective significance of a perception ++ memory: ability to store and retrieve percepts or concepts ++ executive function: anticipation, selection, monitoring of consequences, and initiation of motor activity including praxis, speech.

terms.name: Semiology-elementary-motor
terms.description: A single type of contraction of a muscle or group of muscles that is usually stereotyped and not decomposable into phases. However, see tonic-clonic, an elementary motor sequence.

terms.name: Semiology-myoclonic-jerk
terms.description: Characterized by myoclonus. MYOCLONUS : sudden, brief (lower than 100 ms) involuntary single or multiple contraction(s) of muscles(s) or muscle groups of variable topography (axial, proximal limb, distal).

terms.name: Semiology-negative-myoclonus
terms.description: Characterized by negative myoclonus. NEGATIVE MYOCLONUS: interruption of tonic muscular activity for lower than 500 ms without evidence of preceding myoclonia.

terms.name: Semiology-clonic
terms.description: Myoclonus that is regularly repetitive, involves the same muscle groups, at a frequency of about 2 to 3 c/s, and is prolonged. Synonym: rhythmic myoclonus.

terms.name: Semiology-jacksonian-march
terms.description: Term indicating spread of clonic movements through contiguous body parts unilaterally.

terms.name: Semiology-epileptic-spasm
terms.description: A sudden flexion, extension, or mixed extension flexion of predominantly proximal and truncal muscles that is usually more sustained than a myoclonic movement but not so sustained as a tonic seizure (i.e., about 1 s). Limited forms may occur: grimacing, head nodding. Frequent occurrence in clusters.

terms.name: Semiology-tonic
terms.description: A sustained increase in muscle contraction lasting a few seconds to minutes.

terms.name: Semiology-dystonic
terms.description: Sustained contractions of both agonist and antagonist muscles producing athetoid or twisting movements, which, when prolonged, may produce abnormal postures.

terms.name: Semiology-postural
terms.description: Adoption of a posture that may be bilaterally symmetric or asymmetric (as in a fencing posture).

terms.name: Semiology-versive
terms.description: A sustained, forced conjugate ocular, cephalic, and/or truncal rotation or lateral deviation from the midline.

terms.name: Semiology-tonic-clonic
terms.description: A sequence consisting of a tonic followed by a clonic phase. Variants such as clonic-tonic-clonic may be seen.

terms.name: Semiology-tonic-clonic-without-figure-of-four
terms.description: Without figure of four: Asymmetry of limb posture during the tonic phase of a GTC: one arm is rigidly extended at the elbow (often with the fist clenched tightly and flexed at the wrist), whereas the opposite arm is flexed at the elbow.

terms.name: Semiology-tonic-clonic-with-figure-of-four-extension-left-elbow
terms.description: With figure of four: Asymmetry of limb posture during the tonic phase of a GTC: one arm is rigidly extended at the elbow (often with the fist clenched tightly and flexed at the wrist), whereas the opposite arm is flexed at the elbow.

terms.name: Semiology-tonic-clonic-with-figure-of-four-extension-right-elbow
terms.description: With figure of four: Asymmetry of limb posture during the tonic phase of a GTC: one arm is rigidly extended at the elbow (often with the fist clenched tightly and flexed at the wrist), whereas the opposite arm is flexed at the elbow.

terms.name: Semiology-astatic
terms.description: Loss of erect posture that results from an atonic, myoclonic, or tonic mechanism. Synonym: drop attack.

terms.name: Semiology-atonic
terms.description: Sudden loss or diminution of muscle tone without apparent preceding myoclonic or tonic event lasting greater or equal to 1 to 2 s, involving head, trunk, jaw, or limb musculature.

terms.name: Semiology-automatisms
terms.description: A more or less coordinated, repetitive, motor activity usually occurring when cognition is impaired and for which the subject is usually amnesic afterward. This often resembles a voluntary movement and may consist of an inappropriate continuation of ongoing preictal motor activity.

terms.name: Semiology-mimetic
terms.description: Facial expression suggesting an emotional state, often fear.

terms.name: Semiology-oroalimentary
terms.description: Lip smacking, lip pursing, chewing, licking, tooth grinding, or swallowing.

terms.name: Semiology-dacrystic
terms.description: Bursts of crying.

terms.name: Semiology-manual
terms.description: 1. Indicates principally distal components, bilateral or unilateral. 2. Fumbling, tapping, manipulating movements.

terms.name: Semiology-gestural
terms.description: Semipurposive, asynchronous hand movements. Often unilateral.

terms.name: Semiology-hypermotor
terms.description: 1. Involves predominantly proximal limb or axial muscles producing irregular sequential ballistic movements, such as pedaling, pelvic thrusting, thrashing, rocking movements. 2. Increase in rate of ongoing movements or inappropriately rapid performance of a movement.

terms.name: Semiology-hypokinetic
terms.description: A decrease in amplitude and/or rate or arrest of ongoing motor activity.

terms.name: Semiology-gelastic
terms.description: Bursts of laughter or giggling, usually without an appropriate affective tone.

terms.name: Semiology-sensory
terms.description: A perceptual experience not caused by appropriate stimuli in the external world. Modifies seizure or aura.

terms.name: Semiology-headache
terms.description: Headache occurring in close temporal proximity to the seizure or as the sole seizure manifestation.

terms.name: Semiology-visual
terms.description: Flashing or flickering lights, spots, simple patterns, scotomata, or amaurosis.

terms.name: Semiology-auditory
terms.description: Buzzing, drumming sounds or single tones.

terms.name: Semiology-gustatory
terms.description: Taste sensations including acidic, bitter, salty, sweet, or metallic.

terms.name: Semiology-epigastric
terms.description: Abdominal discomfort including nausea, emptiness, tightness, churning, butterflies, malaise, pain, and hunger; sensation may rise to chest or throat. Some phenomena may reflect ictal autonomic dysfunction.

terms.name: Semiology-somatosensory
terms.description: Tingling, numbness, electric-shock sensation, sense of movement or desire to move.

terms.name: Semiology-autonomic-sensation
terms.description: Viscerosensitive. A sensation consistent with involvement of the autonomic nervous system, including cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, sudomotor, vasomotor, and thermoregulatory functions. (Thus autonomic aura; cf. autonomic events 3.0/Semiology-autonomic).

terms.name: Semiology-experiential
terms.description: Affective, mnemonic, or composite perceptual phenomena including illusory or composite hallucinatory events; these may appear alone or in combination. Included are feelings of depersonalization. These phenomena have subjective qualities similar to those experienced in life but are recognized by the subject as occurring outside of actual context.

terms.name: Semiology-affective-emotional
terms.description: Components include fear, depression, joy, and (rarely) anger.

terms.name: Semiology-hallucinatory
terms.description: Composite perceptions without corresponding external stimuli involving visual, auditory, somatosensory, olfactory, and/or gustatory phenomena. Example: hearing and seeing people talking.

terms.name: Semiology-illusory
terms.description: An alteration of actual percepts involving the visual, auditory, somatosensory, olfactory, or gustatory systems.

terms.name: Semiology-mnemonic
terms.description: Components that reflect ictal dysmnesia such as feelings of familiarity (deja-vu) and unfamiliarity (jamais-vu). Use suggested tags to indicate Familiar (deja-vu) or Unfamiliar (jamais-vu).

terms.name: Semiology-vocalization
terms.description: Single or repetitive utterances consisting of sounds such as grunts or shrieks.

terms.name: Semiology-verbalization
terms.description: Single or repetitive utterances consisting of words, phrases, or brief sentences.

terms.name: Semiology-dysphasia
terms.description: Partially impaired communication involving language without dysfunction of relevant primary motor or sensory pathways, manifested as impaired comprehension, anomia, paraphasic errors, or a combination of these. (

terms.name: Semiology-aphasia
terms.description: Fully impaired communication involving language without dysfunction of relevant primary motor or sensory pathways, manifested as impaired comprehension, anomia, paraphasic errors, or a combination of these.

terms.name: Semiology-autonomic
terms.description: An objectively documented and distinct alteration of autonomic nervous system function involving cardiovascular, pupillary, gastrointestinal, sudomotor, vasomotor, and thermoregularity functions (cf. Semiology-autonomic-sensation).

terms.name: Semiology-pupillary
terms.description: Mydriasis, miosis (either bilateral or unilateral).

terms.name: Semiology-hypersalivation
terms.description: Increase in production of saliva leading to uncontrollable drooling.

terms.name: Semiology-respiratory-apnoeic
terms.description: Subjective shortness of breath, hyperventilation, stridor, coughing, choking, apnea, oxygen desaturation, neurogenic pulmonary edema.

terms.name: Semiology-cardiovascular
terms.description: Modifications of heart rate (tachycardia, bradycardia), cardiac arrhythmias (such as sinus arrhythmia, sinus arrest, supraventricular tachycardia, atrial premature depolarizations, ventricular premature depolarizations, atrio-ventricular block, bundle branch block, atrioventricular nodal escape rhythm, asystole).

terms.name: Semiology-gastrointestinal
terms.description: Nausea, eructation, vomiting, retching, abdominal sensations, abdominal pain, flatulence, spitting, diarrhea.

terms.name: Semiology-urinary-incontinence
terms.description: Urinary urge (intense urinary urge at the beginning of seizures), urinary incontinence, ictal urination (rare symptom of partial seizures without loss of consciousness).

terms.name: Semiology-genital
terms.description: Sexual auras (erotic thoughts and feelings, sexual arousal and orgasm). Genital auras (unpleasant, sometimes painful, frightening or emotionally neutral somatosensory sensations in the genitals that can be accompanied by ictal orgasm). Sexual automatisms (hypermotor movements consisting of writhing, thrusting, rhythmic movements of the pelvis, arms and legs, sometimes associated with picking and rhythmic manipulation of the groin or genitalia, exhibitionism and masturbation).

terms.name: Semiology-vasomotor
terms.description: Flushing or pallor (may be accompanied by feelings of warmth, cold and pain).

terms.name: Semiology-sudomotor
terms.description: Sweating and piloerection (may be accompanied by feelings of warmth, cold and pain).

terms.name: Semiology-thermoregulatory
terms.description: Hyperthermia, fever. (Source: Beniczky ea 2017, Table 10; Beniczky ea 2013, Appendix S5.)

terms.name: Postictal-semiology
terms.description: A transient clinical abnormality of central nervous system function that appears or becomes accentuated when clinical signs of the ictus have ended.

terms.name: Postictal-unconscious
terms.description: Unawareness and unresponsiveness.

terms.name: Postictal-quick-recovery-of-consciousness
terms.description: Quick recovery of awareness and responsiveness. )

terms.name: Postictal-aphasia-or-dysphasia
terms.description: Impaired communication involving language without dysfunction of relevant primary motor or sensory pathways, manifested as impaired comprehension, anomia, parahasic errors or a combination of these.

terms.name: Postictal-behavioral-change
terms.description: Occurring immediately after a seizure. Including psychosis, hypomanina, obsessive-compulsive behavior.

terms.name: Postictal-hemianopia
terms.description: Postictal visual loss in a a hemi field.

terms.name: Postictal-impaired-cognition
terms.description: Decreased Cognitive performance involving one or more of perception, attention, emotion, memory, execution, praxis, speech.

terms.name: Postictal-dysphoria
terms.description: Depression, irritability, euphoric mood, fear, anxiety.

terms.name: Postictal-headache
terms.description: Headache with features of tension-type or migraine headache that develops within 3 h following the seizure and resolves within 72 h after seizure.

terms.name: Postictal-nose-wiping
terms.description: Noes-wiping usually within 60 sec of seizure offset, usually with the hand ipsilateral to the seizure onset.

terms.name: Postictal-anterograde-amnesia
terms.description: Impaired ability to remember new material.

terms.name: Postictal-retrograde-amnesia
terms.description: Impaired ability to recall previously remember material.

terms.name: Postictal-paresis
terms.description: Todds palsy. Any unilateral postictal dysfunction relating to motor, language, sensory and/or integrative functions.

terms.name: Postictal-sleep
terms.description: Invincible need to sleep after a seizure.

terms.name: Postictal-unilateral-myoclonic-jerks
terms.description: Unilateral myoclonic jerks. Myoclonus: sudden, brief (<100 ms) involuntary single or multiple contraction(s) of muscles(s) or muscle groups of variable topography (axial, proximal limb, distal).

terms.name: Postictal-other-unilateral-motor-phenomena
terms.description: Unilateral motor phenomena, other then specified above, occurring in the postictal phase.

terms.name: Episode-time-context-property
terms.description: Additional clinically relevant features related to episodes can be scored under timing and context. If needed, episode duration can be tagged with suggested tag.

terms.name: Episode-awareness
terms.description: False: the patient is not aware of the episode. True: the patient is aware of the episode.

terms.name: Episode-event-count
terms.description: Number of stereotypical episodes during the recording.

terms.name: Status-epilepticus
terms.description: Episode with duration >30 min but not precisely determined (status epilepticus).

terms.name: Episode-prodrome
terms.description: Prodrome is a preictal phenomenon, and it is defined as a subjective or objective clinical alteration (e.g., ill-localized sensation or agitation) that heralds the onset of an epileptic seizure but does not form part of it (Blume ea 2001). Therefore, prodrome should be distinguished from aura (which is an ictal phenomenon). If prodrome present/true + free text.

terms.name: Artifact-significance-to-recording
terms.description: It is important to score the significance of the described artifacts: recording is not interpretable, recording of reduced diagnostic value, does not interfere with the interpretation of the recording.

terms.name: Feature-significance-to-recording
terms.description: Significance of feature. When normal/abnormal could be labeled with with suggested tags.

terms.name: Feature-frequency
terms.description: Value in Hz (number) typed in.

terms.name: Feature-amplitude
terms.description: Value in microvolts (number) typed in, e.g. (Feature-amplitude/number uv)

terms.name: Property-not-possible-to-determine
terms.description: Not possible to determine.

terms.name: Interictal-activity
terms.description: EEG pattern / transient that is distinguished from the background activity, considered abnormal, but is not recorded during ictal period (seizure) or postictal period; the presence of interictal activity does not necessarily imply that the patient has epilepsy.

terms.name: Epileptiform-interictal-activity
terms.description: Transients distinguishable from background activity, with characteristic spiky morphology, typically, but neither exclusively, nor invariably found in interictal EEGs of people with epilepsy.

terms.name: Abnormal-interictal-rhythmic-activity
terms.description: Activity of frequency lower than alpha, that clearly exceeds the amount considered physiologically normal for patient age and state of alertness.

terms.name: Interictal-periodic-discharges
terms.description: Periodic discharge not further specified (PDs).

terms.name: Generalized-periodic-discharges
terms.description: GPDs. The term generalized refers to any bilateral, bisynchronous and symmetric pattern, even if it has a restricted field (e.g. bifrontal).

terms.name: Lateralized-periodic-discharges
terms.description: LPDs. Lateralized includes unilateral and bilateral synchronous but asymmetric; includes focal, regional and hemispheric patterns.

terms.name: Bilateral-independent-periodic-discharges
terms.description: BIPDs. Bilateral Independent refers to the presence of 2 independent (asynchronous) lateralized patterns, one in each hemisphere.

terms.name: Multifocal-periodic-discharges
terms.description: MfPDs. Multifocal refers to the presence of at least three independent lateralized patterns with at least one in each hemisphere.

terms.name: Physiologic-pattern
terms.description: EEG graphoelements or rhythms that are considered normal. They only should be scored if the physician considers that they have a specific clinical significance for the recording.

terms.name: Rhythmic-activity-pattern
terms.description: Rhythmic activity.

terms.name: Slow-alpha-variant-rhythm
terms.description: Characteristic rhythms mostly at 4-5 Hz, recorded most prominently over the posterior regions of the head. The signals generally alternate or are intermixed with the alpha rhythm to which they are often harmonically related. Amplitude varies but is frequently close to 50 micro V. Blocked or attenuated by attention, especially visual, and mental effort. Comment: slow alpha variant rhythms should be distinguished from posterior slow waves characteristic of children and adolescents and occasionally seen in young adults.

terms.name: Fast-alpha-variant-rhythm
terms.description: Characteristic rhythm at 14-20 Hz, detected most prominently over the posterior regions of the head. May alternate or be intermixed with alpha rhythm. Blocked or attenuated by attention, especially visual, and mental effort.

terms.name: Lambda-wave
terms.description: Diphasic sharp transient occurring over occipital regions of the head of waking subjects during visual exploration. The main component is positive relative to other areas. Time-locked to saccadic eye movement. Amplitude varies but is generally below 50 microV.

terms.name: Posterior-slow-waves-youth
terms.description: Waves in the delta and theta range, of variable form, lasting 0.35 to 0.5 s or longer without any consistent periodicity, found in the range of 6-12 years (occasionally seen in young adults). Alpha waves are almost always intermingled or superimposed. Reactive similar to alpha activity.

terms.name: Diffuse-slowing-hyperventilation
terms.description: Bilateral, diffuse slowing of brain signals during hyperventilation. Recorded in 70 percent of normal children (3-5 years) and less then 10 percent of adults. Slowing usually appears in the posterior regions and spreads forward in younger age groups, whereas slowing tends to appear in the frontal regions and spreads backward in the older age group.

terms.name: Photic-driving
terms.description: Physiologic response consisting of rhythmic activity elicited over the posterior regions of the head by repetitive photic stimulation at frequencies of about 5-30 Hz. Comments: term should be limited to activity time-locked to the stimulus and of frequency identical or harmonically related to the stimulus frequency. Photic driving should be distinguished from the visual evoked potentials elicited by isolated flashes of light or flashes repeated at very low frequency.

terms.name: Photomyogenic-response
terms.description: A response to intermittent photic stimulation characterized by the appearance in the record of brief, repetitive muscular artifacts (spikes) over the anterior regions of the head. These often increase gradually in amplitude as stimuli are continued and cease promptly when the stimulus is withdrawn. Comment: this response is frequently associated with flutter of the eyelids and vertical oscillations of the eyeballs and sometimes with discrete jerking mostly involving the musculature of the face and head. (Preferred to synonym: photo-myoclonic response).

terms.name: Arousal-pattern
terms.description: Arousal pattern in children. Prolonged, marked high voltage 4-6/s activity in all leads with some intermixed slower frequencies.

terms.name: Frontal-arousal-rhythm
terms.description: Prolonged (up to 20s) rhythmical sharp or spiky activity over the frontal areas (maximum over the frontal midline) seen at arousal from sleep in children with minimal cerebral dysfunction.

terms.name: Polygraphic-channel-feature
terms.description: Changes observed in polygraphic channels can be scored: EOG, Respiration, ECG, EMG, other polygraphic channel (+ free text), and their significance logged (normal, abnormal, no definite abnormality).

terms.name: EOG-channel-feature
terms.description: Electrooculogram (EOG) channel features.

terms.name: Respiration-channel-feature
terms.description: Findings in respiration sensors.

terms.name: Oxygen-saturation
terms.description: Percentage.

terms.name: Apnea
terms.description: Temporary cessation of breathing. Duration range in seconds.

terms.name: Hypopnea
terms.description: Overly shallow breathing or an abnormally low respiratory rate. Duration (range in seconds).

terms.name: Apnea-hypopnea-index
terms.description: Events/hour as calculated by dividing the number of apnoea and hypopnoea events by the number of hours of sleep.

terms.name: Periodic-respiration
terms.description: Three or more episodes of central apnea lasting at least 4 seconds, separated by no more than 30 seconds of normal breathing.

terms.name: Tachypnea
terms.description: Numerical value for cycles / minute.

terms.name: ECG-channel-feature
terms.description: Findings in Electrocardiogram recordings.

terms.name: ECG-QT-period
terms.description: The time from the start of the Q wave to the end of the T wave

terms.name: ECG-normal-rhythm
terms.description: Normal rhythm.

terms.name: ECG-arrhythmia
terms.description: Free text annotating characteristics of arrythymia.

terms.name: ECG-asystolia
terms.description: Absence of ventricular contractions in the context of a lethal heart arrhythmia. Duration in seconds of the absence.

terms.name: ECG-bradycardia
terms.description: A resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute. Numerical value for frequency in beats/minute.

terms.name: ECG-extrasystole
terms.description: A heart rhythm disorder corresponding to a premature contraction of one of the chambers of the heart.

terms.name: ECG-ventricular-premature-depolarization
terms.description: A premature ventricular contraction (PVC) is a common event where the heartbeat is initiated by Purkinje fibers in the ventricles rather than by the sinoatrial node.

terms.name: ECG-tachycardia
terms.description: A resting heart rate over 100 beats per minute. Numerical value for frequency in beats/minute.

terms.name: EMG-channel-feature
terms.description: Findings in Electromyography recordings. Suggested tags can be used to note the side of the muscle (Left or Right). The order of activation may be indicated using Temporal-relation: (Left, (Before,Right)).

terms.name: Myoclonus-rhythmic
terms.description: Numerical value for frequency.

terms.name: PLMS
terms.description: Periodic limb movements in sleep.

terms.name: Other-polygraphic-channel-feature
terms.description: Add the name and type of the polygraphic channel as well as the feature in the description.

terms.name: Sleep-and-drowsiness
terms.description: The features of the ongoing activity during sleep are scored here. If abnormal graphoelements appear, disappear or change their morphology during sleep, that is not scored here but at the entry corresponding to that graphoelement (as a modulator).

terms.name: Sleep-architecture
terms.description: For longer recordings. Only to be scored if whole-night sleep is part of the recording. It is a global descriptor of the structure and pattern of sleep: estimation of the amount of time spent in REM and NREM sleep, sleep duration, NREM-REM cycle.

terms.name: Normal-sleep-architecture
terms.description: Recording containing sleep-patterns that are considered normal for the attained sleep stages and for the age.

terms.name: Abnormal-sleep-architecture
terms.description: Absence or consistently marked amplitude asymmetry (>50%) of a normal sleep graphoelement.

terms.name: Sleep-stage-reached
terms.description: For normal sleep patterns the sleep stages reached during the recording can be specified.

terms.name: Sleep-stage-N1
terms.description: Sleep stage 1.

terms.name: Sleep-stage-N2
terms.description: Sleep stage 2.

terms.name: Sleep-stage-N3
terms.description: Sleep stage 3.

terms.name: Sleep-stage-REM
terms.description: Rapid eye movement.

terms.name: Sleep-spindles
terms.description: Burst at 11-15 Hz but mostly at 12-14 Hz generally diffuse but of higher voltage over the central regions of the head, occurring during sleep. Amplitude varies but is mostly below 50 microV in the adult.

terms.name: Vertex-wave
terms.description: Sharp potential, maximal at the vertex, negative relative to other areas, apparently occurring spontaneously during sleep or in response to a sensory stimulus during sleep or wakefulness. May be single or repetitive. Amplitude varies but rarely exceeds 250 microV. Abbreviation: V wave. Synonym: vertex sharp wave.

terms.name: K-complex
terms.description: A burst of somewhat variable appearance, consisting most commonly of a high voltage negative slow wave followed by a smaller positive slow wave frequently associated with a sleep spindle. Duration greater than 0.5 s. Amplitude is generally maximal in the frontal vertex. K complexes occur during nonREM sleep, apparently spontaneously, or in response to sudden sensory / auditory stimuli, and are not specific for any individual sensory modality.

terms.name: Saw-tooth-waves
terms.description: Vertex negative 2-5 Hz waves occurring in series during REM sleep.

terms.name: POSTS
terms.description: Positive occipital sharp transients of sleep. Sharp transient maximal over the occipital regions, positive relative to other areas, apparently occurring spontaneously during sleep. May be single or repetitive. Amplitude varies but is generally below 50 microV.

terms.name: Hypnagogic-hypersynchrony
terms.description: Hypnagogic/hypnopompic hypersynchrony in children. Bursts of bilateral, synchronous delta or theta activity of large amplitude, occasionally with superimposed faster components, occurring during falling asleep or during awakening, in children.

terms.name: Non-reactive-sleep
terms.description: EEG activity consisting of normal sleep graphoelements, but which cannot be interrupted by external stimuli/ the patient cannot be wakened.

terms.name: Uncertain-significant-pattern
terms.description: EEG graphoelements or rhythms that resemble abnormal patterns but that are not necessarily associated with a pathology, and the physician does not consider them abnormal in the context of the scored recording (like normal variants and patterns).

terms.name: Sharp-transient-pattern
terms.description: Sharp transient.

terms.name: Wicket-spikes
terms.description: Spike-like monophasic negative single waves or trains of waves occurring over the temporal regions during drowsiness that have an arcuate or mu-like appearance. These are mainly seen in older individuals and represent a benign variant that is of little clinical significance.

terms.name: Small-sharp-spikes
terms.description: Benign Epileptiform Transients of Sleep (BETS). Small Sharp Spikes (SSS) of very short duration and low amplitude, often followed by a small theta wave, occurring in the temporal regions during drowsiness and light sleep. They occur on one or both sides (often asynchronously). The main negative and positive components are of about equally spiky character. Rarely seen in children, they are seen most often in adults and the elderly. Two thirds of the patients have a history of epileptic seizures.

terms.name: Fourteen-six-Hz-positive-burst
terms.description: Burst of arch-shaped waves at 13-17 Hz and/or 5-7-Hz but most commonly at 14 and/or 6 Hz seen generally over the posterior temporal and adjacent areas of one or both sides of the head during sleep. The sharp peaks of its component waves are positive with respect to other regions. Amplitude varies but is generally below 75 micro V. Comments: (1) best demonstrated by referential recording using contralateral earlobe or other remote, reference electrodes. (2) This pattern has no established clinical significance.

terms.name: Six-Hz-spike-slow-wave
terms.description: Spike and slow wave complexes at 4-7 Hz, but mostly at 6 Hz occurring generally in brief bursts bilaterally and synchronously, symmetrically or asymmetrically, and either confined to or of larger amplitude over the posterior or anterior regions of the head. The spike has a strong positive component. Amplitude varies but is generally smaller than that of spike-and slow-wave complexes repeating at slower rates. Comment: this pattern should be distinguished from epileptiform discharges. Synonym: wave and spike phantom.

terms.name: Rudimentary-spike-wave-complex
terms.description: Synonym: pseudo petit mal discharge. Paroxysmal discharge that consists of generalized or nearly generalized high voltage 3 to 4/sec waves with poorly developed spike in the positive trough between the slow waves, occurring in drowsiness only. It is found only in infancy and early childhood when marked hypnagogic rhythmical theta activity is paramount in the drowsy state.

terms.name: Slow-fused-transient
terms.description: A posterior slow-wave preceded by a sharp-contoured potential that blends together with the ensuing slow wave, in children.

terms.name: Needle-like-occipital-spikes-blind
terms.description: Spike discharges of a particularly fast and needle-like character develop over the occipital region in most congenitally blind children. Completely disappear during childhood or adolescence.

terms.name: Subclinical-rhythmic-EEG-discharge-adults
terms.description: Subclinical Rhythmic EEG Discharge of Adults (SERDA). A rhythmic pattern seen in adults, mainly in the waking state or drowsiness. It consists of a mixture of frequencies, often predominant in the theta range. The onset may be fairly abrupt with widespread sharp rhythmical theta and occasionally with delta activity. As to the spatial distribution, a maximum of this discharge is usually found over the centroparietal region and especially over the vertex. It may resemble a seizure discharge but is not accompanied by any clinical signs or symptoms.

terms.name: Rhythmic-temporal-theta-burst-drowsiness
terms.description: Rhythmic temporal theta burst of drowsiness (RTTD). Characteristic burst of 4-7 Hz waves frequently notched by faster waves, occurring over the temporal regions of the head during drowsiness. Synonym: psychomotor variant pattern. Comment: this is a pattern of drowsiness that is of no clinical significance.

terms.name: Ciganek-rhythm
terms.description: Ciganek rhythm (midline central theta)

terms.name: Temporal-slowing-elderly
terms.description: Focal theta and/or delta activity over the temporal regions, especially the left, in persons over the age of 60. Amplitudes are low/similar to the background activity. Comment: focal temporal theta was found in 20 percent of people between the ages of 40-59 years, and 40 percent of people between 60 and 79 years. One third of people older than 60 years had focal temporal delta activity.

terms.name: Breach-rhythm
terms.description: Rhythmical activity recorded over cranial bone defects. Usually it is in the 6 to 11/sec range and does not respond to movements.

terms.name: Data-artifact
terms.description: An anomalous, interfering, or distorting signal originating from a source other than the item being studied.

terms.name: Biological-artifact
terms.description: A data artifact arising from a biological entity being measured.

terms.name: Chewing-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from moving the jaw in a chewing motion.

terms.name: ECG-artifact
terms.description: An electrical artifact from the far-field potential from pulsation of the heart, time locked to QRS complex.

terms.name: EMG-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from muscle activity and myogenic potentials at the measurements site. In EEG, myogenic potentials are the most common artifacts. Frontalis and temporalis muscles (e.g. clenching of jaw muscles) are common causes. Generally, the potentials generated in the muscles are of shorter duration than those generated in the brain. The frequency components are usually beyond 30-50 Hz, and the bursts are arrhythmic.

terms.name: Eye-artifact
terms.description: Ocular movements and blinks can result in artifacts in different types of data. In electrophysiology data, these can result transients and offsets the signal.

terms.name: Eye-blink-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from eye blinking. In EEG, Fp1/Fp2 electrodes become electro-positive with eye closure because the cornea is positively charged causing a negative deflection in Fp1/Fp2. If the eye blink is unilateral, consider prosthetic eye.

terms.name: Eye-movement-artifact
terms.description: Eye movements can cause artifacts on recordings. The charge of the eye can especially cause artifacts in electrophysiology data.

terms.name: Horizontal-eye-movement-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from moving eyes left-to-right and right-to-left. In EEG, there is an upward deflection in the Fp2-F8 derivation, when the eyes move to the right side. In this case F8 becomes more positive and therefore. When the eyes move to the left, F7 becomes more positive and there is an upward deflection in the Fp1-F7 derivation.

terms.name: Nystagmus-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from nystagmus (a vision condition in which the eyes make repetitive, uncontrolled movements).

terms.name: Slow-eye-movement-artifact
terms.description: Artifacts originating from slow, rolling eye-movements, seen during drowsiness.

terms.name: Vertical-eye-movement-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from moving eyes up and down. In EEG, this causes positive potentials (50-100 micro V) with bi-frontal distribution, maximum at Fp1 and Fp2, when the eyeball rotates upward. The downward rotation of the eyeball is associated with the negative deflection. The time course of the deflections is similar to the time course of the eyeball movement.

terms.name: Movement-artifact
terms.description: Artifact in the measured data generated by motion of the subject.

terms.name: Pulse-artifact
terms.description: A mechanical artifact from a pulsating blood vessel near a measurement site, cardio-ballistic artifact.

terms.name: Respiration-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from breathing.

terms.name: Rocking-patting-artifact
terms.description: Quasi-rhythmical artifacts in recordings most commonly seen in infants. Typically caused by a caregiver rocking or patting the infant.

terms.name: Sucking-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from sucking, typically seen in very young cases.

terms.name: Sweat-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from sweating. In EEG, this is a low amplitude undulating waveform that is usually greater than 2 seconds and may appear to be an unstable baseline.

terms.name: Tongue-movement-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from tongue movement (Glossokinetic). The tongue functions as a dipole, with the tip negative with respect to the base. In EEG, the artifact produced by the tongue has a broad potential field that drops from frontal to occipital areas, although it is less steep than that produced by eye movement artifacts. The amplitude of the potentials is greater inferiorly than in parasagittal regions; the frequency is variable but usually in the delta range. Chewing and sucking can produce similar artifacts.

terms.name: Nonbiological-artifact
terms.description: A data artifact arising from a non-biological source.

terms.name: Artificial-ventilation-artifact
terms.description: Artifact stemming from mechanical ventilation. These can occur at the same rate as the ventilator, but also have other patterns.

terms.name: Dialysis-artifact
terms.description: Artifacts seen in recordings during continuous renal replacement therapy (dialysis).

terms.name: Electrode-movement-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from electrode movement.

terms.name: Electrode-pops-artifact
terms.description: Brief artifact with a steep rise and slow fall of an electrophysiological signal, most often caused by a loose electrode.

terms.name: Induction-artifact
terms.description: Artifacts induced by nearby equipment. In EEG, these are usually of high frequency.

terms.name: Line-noise-artifact
terms.description: Power line noise at 50 Hz or 60 Hz.

terms.name: Salt-bridge-artifact
terms.description: Artifact from salt-bridge between EEG electrodes.
